content: Umbilical arterial catheters (UACs) are widely used in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) for monitoring critically ill newborns. However, there is considerable variability in how these catheters are utilized across different NICUs. This variability includes differences in the use of heparin, the materials and design of the catheters, and their positioning. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate whether adding heparin to the fluids infused through UACs in newborns has an impact on several clinical outcomes. These outcomes include the frequency of catheter occlusion, aortic thrombosis, intraventricular hemorrhage, hypertension, death, clinical ischemic events, and the duration of catheter usability. To address this question, randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials were reviewed. The search for relevant studies was conducted using databases such as The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CINAHL, and EMBASE, covering the period from 1999 to 2009. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized trials involving newborns of any birthweight or gestational age. The studies compared the use of heparinized infusion fluids to non-heparinized fluids, as well as heparin in the infusate versus heparin only in the flush solution. Key clinical endpoints included catheter occlusion and aortic thrombosis. Five randomized controlled trials were identified and analyzed. All of these studies reported data on the incidence of catheter occlusion, and two of them also provided information on the occurrence of aortic thrombosis. In most of the trials, the intervention involved adding heparin to the infusate at a concentration of 1 unit/mL, except for one study that used a lower concentration of 0.25 units/mL. The studies included both term and preterm infants. The results demonstrated that heparinization of the infusate significantly reduces the incidence of catheter occlusion. However, it does not appear to influence the frequency of aortic thrombosis. Using heparin only in the flush solution, without heparinizing the infusate, was found to be ineffective in preventing catheter occlusion. Additionally, there was no evidence to suggest that heparinization of the infusate affects the rates of intraventricular hemorrhage, death, or clinical ischemic events. It is important to note, however, that the confidence intervals for these outcomes were wide, meaning that even substantial effects on these outcomes could not be reliably detected. In conclusion, adding heparin to the fluid infused through UACs reduces the likelihood of catheter occlusion. The lowest effective concentration tested so far is 0.25 units/mL. Heparinization of the flush solution alone is not sufficient to prevent occlusion. The available evidence does not indicate an effect on the frequency of aortic thrombosis, intraventricular hemorrhage, or other clinical outcomes, but the data are not robust enough to rule out significant effects on these endpoints.
